numerics-gan-skew-scale.title: The Numerics of GANs
numerics-gan-skew-scale.version: arXiv:1705.10461v3, 11 June 2018; NeurIPS 2017 main paper and author-hosted supplement
numerics-gan-skew-scale.summary: Consensus regularization changes the local training matrix from A to A−γAᵀA. Lemma 9 bounds how much oscillation remains relative to decay, but its derivation drops the scale of the skew part of A. For A=[(−1,−1),(1,−1)] and γ=1, the eigenvalues after regularization are −3±i. Their imaginary-to-real ratio is 1/3, above the claimed bound of 1/5. Keeping ‖A−Aᵀ‖₂ in the estimate repairs this bound and preserves the conclusion that sufficiently strong damping reduces the ratio.

checks.location: Lemma 9, Eq.(17)–(18) PDF p.6; proof Appendix p.14; Lemma7 proof p.14
checks.claim: Lemma 9 bounds the largest imaginary-to-real eigenvalue ratio of A−γAᵀA using a ratio c formed from the symmetric and skew parts of A, the smallest-singular-value lower bound ρ, and γ.
checks.explanation: The proof divides by the skew quadratic form but drops the same divisor from the regularization term. That form has no assumed unit bound. The resulting estimate fails even for a strictly dissipative $2\times2$ matrix. Restoring its scale repairs the estimate and retains the conclusion that increasing $\gamma$ can make the ratio arbitrarily small.
checks.demonstration: Let $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $A=-I+J$. Then $A+A^\top=-2I$ and $A^\top A=2I$, so $A$ satisfies the assumptions with $\rho=\sqrt2$. For a complex unit vector $v$, the symmetric numerator is $2$, while $|v^*(A-A^\top)v|\leq2$. Equality holds at an eigenvector of $J$, hence $c=1$. At $\gamma=1$, the matrix $A-A^\top A=-3I+J$ has eigenvalues $-3\pm i$. Therefore $$q(1)=\frac13>\frac15=\frac{1}{c+2\rho^2}.$$ This matrix is the ascent–descent Jacobian of the smooth zero-sum payoff $f(x,y)=-x^2/2-xy+y^2/2$, with ascent in $x$ and descent in $y$.
checks.repair: Keep the skew scale $s=\|A-A^\top\|_2$. When $s>0$, define $c$ as the infimum of the original ratio over complex unit vectors with nonzero skew form. For a unit eigenvector $v$ of $B=A-\gamma A^\top A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$, put $a=-v^*(A+A^\top)v\geq0$ and $b=|v^*(A-A^\top)v|$. If $b>0$, the exact identity is $$\frac{|\operatorname{Im}\lambda|}{|\operatorname{Re}\lambda|}=\frac{b}{a+2\gamma\|Av\|^2}=\frac{1}{a/b+2\gamma\|Av\|^2/b}\leq\frac{1}{c+2\gamma\rho^2/s}.$$ Eigenvectors with $b=0$ have zero imaginary part. If $s=0$, $B$ is symmetric and $q(\gamma)=0$. This correction is valid under the original matrix assumptions and is sharp for the displayed example.
checks.scope: The defect concerns the quantitative estimate in Lemma 9. The example satisfies strict negativity of the symmetric part, so singularity and borderline stability do not explain the violation. The correction leaves the consensus update unchanged.
checks.whyItMatters: The printed bound understates the oscillation remaining after consensus regularization. The corrected bound supports the same qualitative damping conclusion, with the matrix-dependent scale included.
checks.title: The consensus damping bound omits the scale of the skew part
checks.claimContext: For an invertible real matrix $A$ with negative semidefinite symmetric part, $\|Av\|\geq\rho\|v\|$ with $\rho>0$, and $\gamma>0$, Lemma 9 bounds $q(\gamma)$, the largest ratio of absolute imaginary to absolute real eigenvalue parts of $A-\gamma A^\top A$. Its quantity $c$ is the infimum of $|v^*(A+A^\top)v|/|v^*(A-A^\top)v|$ over complex unit vectors. Here $v^*$ denotes conjugate transpose.
checks.checkedLocation: Lemma 9, Eqs. (17)–(18), PDF p. 6; proof, Eqs. (26)–(32), PDF p. 14.

Lemma 9 bounds how much oscillation remains relative to decay, but its derivation drops the scale of the skew part of A. For A=[(−1,−1),(1,−1)] and γ=1, the eigenvalues after regularization are −3±i. Their imaginary-to-real ratio is 1/3, above the claimed bound of 1/5. numerics-gan-skew-scale.paperSummary: The Numerics of GANs studies training as a dynamical system in which two networks continually respond to one another. It connects poor local convergence to properties of the combined gradient's Jacobian and proposes consensus optimization, which adds a penalty based on the size of that gradient. The aim is to reduce unstable or strongly oscillatory behavior near an equilibrium.
numerics-gan-skew-scale.theoryRole: Lemma 9 quantifies how consensus regularization changes the ratio of oscillation to decay in the local linear dynamics. This numerical estimate supports the paper's explanation of improved damping; it is distinct from the preceding qualitative local-convergence argument.

The first-order term is \(I-P\), so \(\|E_t\|_2=(1-1/t)^t\to e^{-1}\). The claimed upper bound is \(C/t\to0\). These gates lie strictly between zero and one, the keys are perfectly concentrated, and \(\sum_j\beta_j=1\). The remainder therefore need not vanish even when the total gate mass is one.
checks.repair:
A valid bound follows directly from contraction. Fix the ordering \(M_j=D_jM_{j-1}\), let \(B_j=\sum_{i\leq j}\beta_iP_i\), and write \(M_j=I-B_j+E_j\). Then
\[E_j=D_jE_{j-1}+\beta_jP_jB_{j-1}.\]
Because \(\|D_j\|_2\leq1\) and \(\|P_j\|_2=1\), induction yields
\[\|E_t\|_2\leq\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq t}\beta_i\beta_j\leq\frac{t(t-1)}2\beta_{\max}^2\leq\frac12\Bigl(\sum_j\beta_j\Bigr)^2.\]
The same argument applies to the reverse ordering. A total gate sum tending to zero therefore gives a small absolute remainder; a merely bounded sum does not give the printed \(Ct\beta_{\max}^2\) rate.
checks.scope: The uniform quantitative remainder estimate is false. The product expansion itself is valid, and the corrected pairwise bound supplies a meaningful small-total-gate approximation. This does not establish the later replacement of the product by a centering projection.
checks.claimContext: Lemmas 3 and 6 expand the product of rank-one contractions \(D_j=I-\beta_j k_jk_j^\top\), with unit keys and \(0<\beta_j<1\), around its first-order term. The asserted remainder bound uses a constant \(C\) independent of the prefix length \(t\) and the admissible gates. The proof counts higher-order products and then replaces their dependence on \(t\) by a linear factor.
checks.whyItMatters: The remainder controls the central first-order approximation. Its dependence on all gate interactions must be retained before using that approximation in the attention argument.
checks.title: The product remainder need not be linear in the sequence length
checks.verificationNote: The arXiv:2607.07706v1 product bound is contradicted by aligned unit keys with beta=1/t. The independent verifier rejected the bounded-total-gate repair while retaining the original bound error; the corrected pairwise remainder estimate is stated here.

checks.explanation: Concentration of key directions does not determine the contraction magnitude along their common direction. checks.demonstration:
In dimension one, let every key and the query equal one, every value equal one, and \(\beta_j=1/t\). All logits are equal, so softmax is exactly uniform and its output is one. Centering the keys gives zero, and the exact softmax Taylor remainder along this constant-logit direction is zero. Yet \(M_t=(1-1/t)^t\), so the output implied by equation (11) is
\[\sum_{i=1}^t\left(\frac1t+\frac{(1-1/t)^t}{t}\right)=1+(1-1/t)^t\longrightarrow1+e^{-1}.\]
Perfect concentration and \(\sum_j\beta_j=1\) hold, but the operator mismatch does not vanish.
checks.repair:
For aligned keys, the exact identity is \(M_t=(I-P)+a_tP\), where \(a_t=\prod_j(1-\beta_j)\). Thus \(\|M_t-(I-P)\|_2=a_t\), and the necessary contraction condition is \(a_t\to0\), not normalization of the first-order sum. More generally, bound \(\delta_t=\|M_t-(I-\Pi_{\bar k})\|_2\) directly. If \(k_i-\bar k=(I-\Pi_{\bar k})k_i+r_i\) and \(\epsilon_i\) is the exact first-order softmax remainder, unit keys give
\[\left|P_i^{\mathrm{full}}-\frac1t-\frac{q^\top M_tk_i}{t\sqrt d}\right|\leq |\epsilon_i|+\frac{\|q\|_2}{t\sqrt d}(\|r_i\|_2+\delta_t).\]
This follows by subtracting the two formulas and applying Cauchy–Schwarz. An approximation claim must control all three terms. Matching a gated, suffix-dependent GDN coefficient additionally requires its own factors and ranges from the exact unrolling.
checks.scope: The unjustified step is the quantitative replacement of the centering operator. A structural similarity between rank-one key operations remains possible. The argument does not show that a learned GDN cannot approximate attention; it shows that key concentration and first-order coefficient normalization alone do not prove that approximation.
checks.claimContext: The centered softmax expansion uses \(I-\Pi_{\bar k}\), where \(\Pi_{\bar k}\) projects onto the mean key. Lemma 3 instead describes the key product as approximately \(I-c\Pi_{\bar k}\) for an unspecified \(c\geq0\). The text then substitutes the full product \(M_t\) for the centering operator to obtain equation (11).
checks.whyItMatters: The product must contract the mean-key direction by the correct amount before it can replace softmax centering.

review-neurips-2026-151465.title: Diffusion Guidance Is a Controllable Policy Improvement Operator

checks.explanation: Larger exponents favor actions with higher advantage under the original policy $\hat\pi$. After the policy changes, those advantages need not give the action ordering required for improvement from the new policy. Equation (43) still uses $A_{\hat\pi}$, whereas applying the policy-improvement lemma to $\pi_{w_1}$ requires $A_{\pi_{w_1}}$.
checks.demonstration:
Take a two-state deterministic MDP with discount $\gamma=0.9$. At state zero, action $a$ earns $0.2$ and stays, whereas action $b$ earns zero and moves to state one. At state one, both actions stay; their rewards are $10$ and zero. Let the reference probabilities be
$$\hat\pi(\cdot\mid0)=(0.5,0.5),\qquad \hat\pi(\cdot\mid1)=(0.01,0.99).$$
Its Bellman equations give $V_{\hat\pi}(1)=0.1/(1-0.9)=1$ and $V_{\hat\pi}(0)=0.1+0.9[0.5V_{\hat\pi}(0)+0.5]=1$. Therefore
$$A_{\hat\pi}(0,\cdot)=(0.1,-0.1),\qquad A_{\hat\pi}(1,\cdot)=(9.9,-0.1).$$
Choose $f(x)=(1+e^{-x})^{-1}$, which is bounded, strictly positive and increasing. Both tilted policies have full support. Write
$$p_w=\pi_w(a\mid0)=f(0.1w),$$
$$q_w=\pi_w(a\mid1)=\frac{0.01f(9.9)^w}{0.01f(9.9)^w+0.99f(-0.1)^w}.$$
The tilted policy values solve
$$V_w(1)=100q_w,\qquad V_w(0)=\frac{0.2p_w+0.9(1-p_w)V_w(1)}{1-0.9p_w}.$$
For $w=10$, the action probabilities are approximately $(p_{10},q_{10})=(0.73105858,0.94523307)$, giving $V_{10}(0)=67.31619409$. For $w=20$, they are $(p_{20},q_{20})=(0.88079708,0.99996609)$, giving $V_{20}(0)=52.60478713$. With initial state zero,
$$J(\pi_{10})>J(\pi_{20}),$$
contrary to the claimed monotonicity. Both values exceed the original reference value one, so Theorem 1's improvement over the reference is not contradicted. Expected reference advantages also increase at both states: approximately $(0.04621,9.35233)$ at $w=10$ and $(0.07616,9.89966)$ at $w=20$. That surrogate monotonicity does not order the returns.

The construction also meets a state-only reward convention. Replace each original transition by two steps with discount $\delta=\sqrt{0.9}$. The first enters one of four intermediate states, whose reward is the original action reward divided by $\delta$; the second reaches the original destination. Original decision states have reward zero, and intermediate-state actions are identical. Each original reward contribution is still $\delta(r/\delta)=r$, and the discount between decisions is still $\delta^2=0.9$. Thus this six-state realization preserves the decision-state values, advantages and strict reversal.
checks.repair:
For the fixed-reference family, retain the monotonicity of the reference-advantage surrogate
$$m_s(w)=\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi_w(\cdot\mid s)}A_{\hat\pi}(s,a).$$
With finitely many actions and positive nondecreasing $f$, differentiation gives
$$m_s'(w)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_w}\!\left(A_{\hat\pi},\log f(A_{\hat\pi})\right)\geq0.$$
The inequality follows because the two covariance arguments are ordered in the same way. Each well-defined product policy also improves on $\hat\pi$ by Theorem 1. These facts do not compare returns at two guidance strengths.

For successive return improvement in a finite discounted MDP with bounded rewards, recompute the advantage of the current policy and set
$$\pi'(a\mid s)\propto\pi(a\mid s)f(A_\pi(s,a)),$$
where $f$ is nonnegative, nondecreasing, and has a finite positive normalizer at every state. Since $\mathbb E_\pi A_\pi=0$,
$$g(s):=\mathbb E_{\pi'}A_\pi(s,\cdot)
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(A_\pi,f(A_\pi))}{\mathbb E_\pi f(A_\pi)}\geq0.$$
The Bellman identity then yields
$$V_{\pi'}-V_\pi=(I-\gamma P_{\pi'})^{-1}g
=\sum_{t\geq0}\gamma^tP_{\pi'}^t g\geq0.$$
This is a valid improvement update, but it requires re-evaluating the advantage after each policy change instead of keeping the original reference advantage fixed.
checks.scope: The affected assertions are Theorem 2 and Remark 2's universal ordering of returns by guidance strength. Theorem 1's improvement over the original reference remains consistent with the counterexample.
checks.title: Increasing fixed-reference guidance can lower return
checks.whyItMatters: Increasing guidance can improve the fixed-reference advantage surrogate while reducing the return that the theorem claims to control.
checks.claimContext: Theorem 2 compares the fixed-reference policies $\pi_w(a\mid s)\propto\hat\pi(a\mid s)f(A_{\hat\pi}(s,a))^w$ at $0\le w_1\le w_2$, for bounded nonnegative nondecreasing $f$. It claims that larger guidance strength always gives at least as much discounted return.
checks.checkedLocation: Remark 2; Appendix A, Theorem 2, equations (40)-(43)

checks.claim: The policies that maximize Equation 4 under a given KL-penalty $\beta$ take the form of
checks.explanation: The displayed Gibbs policy exactly optimizes a statewise advantage-and-KL surrogate. Full discounted control also changes future action choices and state visitation. Its optimizer depends on the regularized optimal continuation value, which is generally different from the unregularized value of the fixed reference policy.
checks.demonstration:
Consider a three-state discounted MDP with $\gamma=0.9$, initial state zero, two actions $a,b$, and a uniform reference policy. Each table entry is $(\text{next state},\text{reward})$:
$$\begin{array}{c|cc}
s&a&b\\\hline
0&(0,0)&(1,-4)\\
1&(2,4)&(0,-2)\\
2&(0,-2)&(2,2)
\end{array}$$
The reference value is $(-8.525,-5.975,-6.975)$, giving
$$A_{\hat\pi}=\begin{pmatrix}0.8525&-0.8525\\3.6975&-3.6975\\-2.6975&2.6975\end{pmatrix}.$$
At $\beta=1$, equation (6) assigns action $a$ probabilities approximately
$$p=(0.84618664,\;0.99938606,\;0.00451871).$$
Let $d^\pi=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t\geq0}\gamma^t\Pr_\pi(S_t=\cdot)$ denote normalized discounted occupancy. For this policy, the reward vector is $r_\pi=(-4(1-p_0),6p_1-2,2-4p_2)$ and the statewise KL is $k_i=p_i\log(2p_i)+(1-p_i)\log(2(1-p_i))$. Equation (4) is obtained by solving
$$U=r_\pi-(1-\gamma)k+\gamma P_\pi U.$$
It gives reward return $9.89023857$, occupancy-weighted KL $0.49418025$, and objective $U(0)=9.39605832$.

Now use the deterministic policy $(b,a,b)$. Its reward return is
$$-4+0.9\cdot4+0.9^2\frac{2}{1-0.9}=15.8.$$
Its KL relative to the uniform reference is $\log2$ at every state, so its equation (4) value is
$$15.8-\log2=15.10685282>9.39605832.$$
A strictly better feasible policy suffices to refute the claimed optimizer; no global optimization oracle is needed.

The example also admits state-only rewards. Replace each transition by two steps with discount $\delta=\sqrt{0.9}$, inserting an intermediate state with the original reward divided by $\delta$ and two identical actions. Both policies equal the reference at intermediate states, and decision-state rewards are zero. Decision-state values and reference advantages are unchanged, while normalized KL penalties are multiplied by $1/(1+\delta)$. The two objectives become $9.63664156$ and $15.44429973$, preserving the strict inequality.
checks.repair:
For a finite action space, $\beta>0$, full-support reference policy, and bounded fixed advantage $A_{\hat\pi}$, put
$$Z_s=\sum_a\hat\pi(a\mid s)e^{A_{\hat\pi}(s,a)/\beta},\qquad
\pi_\beta(a\mid s)=\frac{\hat\pi(a\mid s)e^{A_{\hat\pi}(s,a)/\beta}}{Z_s}.$$
The exact identity
$$\mathbb E_\pi A_{\hat\pi}(s,\cdot)-\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\Vert\hat\pi)
=\beta\log Z_s-\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\Vert\pi_\beta)$$
proves that equation (6) maximizes this local surrogate, and hence its average under any fixed state distribution. State that objective explicitly if this is the intended claim.

To retain the full discounted-control objective, use the regularized optimal value. With normalized occupancy set $\lambda=\beta(1-\gamma)$; with unnormalized discounted visitation set $\lambda=\beta$. For finite state and action spaces, bounded rewards, $0\leq\gamma<1$, and a full-support reference, solve
$$Q_\lambda^*(s,a)=r(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb E_{s'\mid s,a}V_\lambda^*(s'),$$
$$V_\lambda^*(s)=\lambda\log\sum_a\hat\pi(a\mid s)e^{Q_\lambda^*(s,a)/\lambda}.$$
The same statewise identity supplies the maximizing policy
$$\pi_\lambda^*(a\mid s)\propto\hat\pi(a\mid s)e^{Q_\lambda^*(s,a)/\lambda}.$$
The soft Bellman operator is a $\gamma$-contraction, so its fixed point gives the regularized control optimum. In general its $Q_\lambda^*$ cannot be replaced by $A_{\hat\pi}$.
checks.scope: The affected assertion is Remark 3 identifying equation (6) as an optimizer of equation (4). The fixed-reference Gibbs policy remains the exact optimizer of the local surrogate and can improve over the reference. This issue is distinct from Theorem 2's claim of monotonic return as guidance increases.
checks.whyItMatters: The claimed optimizer can have substantially lower objective value than another admissible policy, even with exact reference advantages and finite deterministic dynamics.
checks.claimContext: Remark 3 identifies the policy in equation (6), formed by exponentiating the fixed reference advantage $A_{\hat\pi}$, as an optimizer of equation (4). That objective evaluates the candidate policy over full trajectories and uses its own discounted state occupancy in the KL penalty.
checks.title: The Gibbs tilt optimizes a local surrogate, not the stated control objective
checks.checkedLocation: arXiv v1 · Section 3, equations (1)–(4); Section 4, Remark 3 and equation (6).

review-neurips-2026-151520.title: DD-CAM: Minimal Sufficient Explanations for Vision Models Using Delta Debugging

checks.claim: 1-minimality for optimized search
checks.explanation: Additive logits do not make top-1 prediction preservation monotone under deletion. A unit that was necessary when first tested can become redundant after another unit is removed. Signed class-margin contributions are allowed by a linear classifier, so the one-pass optimization lacks the condition needed for its 1-minimality guarantee.
checks.demonstration:
Take three nonnegative unit activations $x_0=x_1=x_2=1$ and a homogeneous binary linear head with target logit $z_c=\tfrac34x_0+x_1-\tfrac54x_2$ and competing logit zero. Test the units in order $0,1,2$. The initial target margin is $1/2$. Removing unit $0$ gives margin $-1/4$, so it is retained. Removing unit $1$ next gives margin $-1/2$, so it is retained too. Removing unit $2$ leaves margin $7/4$, so it is deleted and the pass stops at $\{0,1\}$.

Deleting either remaining unit now preserves the target class: the margins are $1$ and $3/4$, respectively. The returned set is therefore sufficient but not 1-minimal. All comparisons are strict, and the construction uses neither biases nor negative activations.
checks.repair: Repeat deletion passes until a complete pass removes nothing, or use the paper's recursive procedure. Each successful deletion preserves the target class and decreases the finite set size, so the process terminates; the final complete pass certifies that every remaining singleton deletion fails. This proves 1-minimality, not minimum cardinality, with up to $O(M^2)$ tests in the worst case. A one-pass guarantee is valid if the preservation predicate is upward closed: $P(S)=1$ and $S\subseteq T$ imply $P(T)=1$. Then a failed deletion cannot become successful after further removals. Nonnegative contributions to every target-versus-competitor margin are one sufficient condition; logit additivity alone is not.
checks.scope: The failure concerns the optimized one-pass search for GAP-linear heads. The source's recursive delta-debugging procedure retains its 1-minimality guarantee. The counterexample uses a homogeneous linear head, nonnegative activations and strict class comparisons.
checks.title: One deletion pass can return a set that is not 1-minimal
checks.claimContext: DD-CAM seeks a prediction-preserving set for which removing any retained unit changes the predicted class. Sections 5.2.1 and 6.2 claim that an additive, global-average-pooling linear head permits a single sequential deletion pass, testing each unit once without restarting. General recursive delta debugging instead retests after reductions.
checks.whyItMatters: A saliency set cannot be called 1-minimal merely because every retained unit was necessary at an earlier stage of deletion.
checks.checkedLocation: Sections 5.2.1 and 6.2, one-pass optimization for additive GAP-linear heads; prediction-preserving subset definition in Section 5.

Equation2 maps each token feature through an MLP to M_k channels, with an M-by-M_k bias; W_i transpose times x_i correctly gives M_k-by-D representative tokens. $$
\operatorname{Var}_X(\mathbb E[N\mid X])=0,\qquad\operatorname{Var}_X(\mathbb E[S\mid X])=\frac{(\log2)^2}{4}>0.

This is on par with or above VLA models that are more than an order of magnitude larger, such as ARTEMIS [7] (7B), DriveVLA-W0 [23] (7B), ReCogDrive [25] (2B), AdaThinkDrive [30] (2B), and AutoVLA [53] (3B), and surpasses the 8B-scale DriveFine [4] ( $91.8$ ) by $0.4$ points.

These results have two implications.
First, since the only difference from the OpenDriveVLA* baseline is our next visual state prediction and IK Network, the $+19.0$ PDMS and $+20.4$ EPDMS gains are attributable entirely to these two components rather than to model size or data.
Second, the fact that a 0.5B light model has reached driving performance on par with 7B–8B VLAs suggests that structural changes that force active use of visual features may have a greater impact on trajectory planning accuracy than simply scaling up the LLM.

review-neurips-2026-153225.title: Stability and Diversity of Networked Self-Consuming Generative Ecosystems

checks.location: Appendix D.1 Lemma D.1 and D.4/Theorem3.7; work/text/153225.txt:993
checks.claim: The locally unique optimizer is the globally selected Eq.(1) update and is C1 near the fixed point, permitting Theorem3.7.
checks.explanation: Strong concavity near $\bar\theta_i$ isolates a nearby stationary point, but does not rule out a distant likelihood maximum. A small change in a parent distribution can make that distant maximum strictly better. The implicit-function theorem follows the nearby stationary point; without a global objective gap, it does not control the globally selected retraining map.
checks.demonstration:
Consider two models on $\mathbb R^2$, both with covariance $I_2$, synthetic weights $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1$, and parent matrix $W=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Model 1 has parameter space $(-2,2)\cup(8,12)$ and mean $(\theta,1)$ on the first component and $(\theta-10,-1)$ on the second. Model 2 has mean $(0,\eta-1/4)$ with $\eta\in\mathbb R$. Their real-data distributions are $\mathcal N((0,1/4),I_2)$ and $\mathcal N((0,-3/2),I_2)$, respectively. The uncoupled real-data maximizers are unique: $\theta=0$ and $\eta=-5/4$.

At $\bar\Theta=(0,0)$, model 1's global maximizers are $\theta=0$ and $\theta=10$. The paper's nearest-previous-iterate tie-break selects $0$. Model 2's maximizing vertical mean is $(-3/2+1)/2=-1/4$, corresponding to parameter $\eta=0$. Thus $\bar\Theta$ is a fixed point of the actual global update.

On neighborhoods of this fixed point, both real-data log-likelihood Hessians equal $-1$ and are independent of the sampled observation. Thus Assumptions 3.3–3.4 hold with $\alpha_i=1$ and $L_i=0$. The cross-score expectations are zero: they are expectations of a horizontal Gaussian coordinate times a vertical coordinate under distributions with independent coordinates and zero horizontal mean. Hence $M_i=\beta_i=0$ and $\rho(D)=0$.

Now start at $(0,-\varepsilon)$ for any sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$. Model 1's remote branch has objective advantage $2\varepsilon$, so its unique global maximizer is $10$. Model 2 uses the previous near branch and updates to $0$. The next update is $(10,-1)$, which is a fixed point. Therefore
$$(0,-\varepsilon)\longmapsto(10,0)\longmapsto(10,-1)\longmapsto(10,-1).$$
Arbitrarily close initializations leave the neighborhood and never approach $\bar\Theta$. The global update is not continuous there, despite the comparison matrix being zero. The local critical-point branch provided by the implicit-function theorem is a different map.
checks.repair:
Add a global isolation condition that prevents distant maximizers from competing with the local branch. A concrete sufficient version uses compact parameter sets, jointly continuous objectives, and a positive gap
$$H_i(\bar\theta_i;\bar\Theta)>\sup_{\theta_i\notin U_i}H_i(\theta_i;\bar\Theta)+\delta_i,\qquad\delta_i>0,$$
where $\bar\theta_i$ lies in the interior of a convex neighborhood $U_i$ on which the objective is strongly concave. Also require the joint differentiability needed for the implicit-function theorem.

Uniform continuity on the compact parameter set preserves this gap for all parent parameters sufficiently near $\bar\Theta$. The local maximizing branch remains near $\bar\theta_i$, while every point outside $U_i$ remains strictly worse. Consequently, the globally selected update equals the unique local branch and is continuously differentiable. The paper's block-Jacobian bound now applies to the actual update. If $\rho(D)<1$, choose a positive vector $w$ with $Dw<w$; continuity gives a neighborhood in which the update contracts the associated weighted block norm. This proves local convergence for the globally selected map under the added isolation condition.

The condition has a concrete effect in the example. Increasing model 1's real-data vertical mean by $d>0$, while leaving the other ingredients fixed, gives the near branch an advantage $2(d+\eta)$, uniformly positive for $|\eta|\le d/2$. Both models then update to the nearby fixed point. Merely breaking a tie by proximity does not provide this protection when a distant branch becomes strictly better.
checks.scope: Theorem 3.7 fails for the global update under its stated local assumptions, even when $\rho(D)=0$. The added isolation and joint-regularity conditions restore local convergence for that update.
checks.claimContext: Equation (1) defines retraining by a global likelihood maximizer, resolving ties by distance to the previous iterate. Theorem 3.7 claims local convergence to a fixed point $\bar\Theta$ when the comparison matrix $D$ has spectral radius $\rho(D)<1$. The displayed rate uses the local update Jacobian $J$. Its proof must therefore show that this local update is the global maximizer selected by Equation (1).
checks.whyItMatters: The matrix $D$ can predict no local amplification, with $\rho(D)=0$, while the defined retraining rule jumps to a remote fixed point from arbitrarily close starts. A global objective gap is needed to connect the local derivative calculation to the selected likelihood maximizer.

For an explicit example, write $x=(z,y)\in\mathbb R^{100}\times\mathbb R$ and use the flat constraint manifold $\mathcal M=\{z=0\}$. On the manifold, let $y_0$ have equal Gaussian components $\mathcal N(-10,1)$ and $\mathcal N(10,1)$. This satisfies the paper's two-mode assumption with within-mode standard deviation $1$ and total tangential variance $101$, although Theorem 2 does not require that assumption. At $t=\log2$, the safe-phase boundary, the coordinates satisfy
$$z\sim\mathcal N(0,\tfrac12I_{100}),\qquad Y\sim\tfrac12\mathcal N(-m,1)+\tfrac12\mathcal N(m,1),\qquad m=\sqrt{50}.$$
Their scores and velocities are
$$s_z=-2z,\quad s_y=-Y+m\tanh(mY),\qquad v_z=z/2,\quad v_y=-m\tanh(mY)/2.$$
There is a positive solution $y_*$ of $y_*=m\tanh(my_*)$. At $(0,y_*)$ the score is zero but $v_y=-y_*/2\ne0$. Thus no scalar $A_t$ can make the asserted score-only step describe this flow; its error is of order $\Delta t$, not an Euler remainder of order $\Delta t^2$.

To measure the consequence, use linear blocks with Jacobians $J_1=\operatorname{diag}(0.001I_{100},0.999)$ and $J_2=\operatorname{diag}(0.002I_{100},0.998)$. They satisfy the positive unit-gain bounds and depth ordering; the manifold has infinite reach, and smoothness, finite moments and temporal regularity hold on a sufficiently small positive-time cache window. The actual ODE has the required fourth-moment Euler remainder. Let $I=\mathbb E s_y^2$. Integration by parts gives $I=1-m^2\mathbb E\operatorname{sech}^2(mY)\le1$. Using the usual VP score coefficient $|A_t|=1/2$ would give the claimed leading coefficient
$$2B\Theta_t=\tfrac12\bigl[200(0.001)^2+(0.999)^2I\bigr]\le0.4991005.$$
The true coefficient is
$$\mathbb E\|J_1v_t\|^2=\frac{100(0.001)^2}{8}+\frac{50(0.999)^2}{4}\mathbb E\tanh^2(mY)>11.47.$$
For the last inequality, a draw lies within $m/2$ of its component mean with probability at least $1-4/m^2=0.92$ by Chebyshev's inequality; on that event $|mY|\ge25$. Numerical quadrature gives approximately $12.4750$ for the actual coefficient and $0.4991005$ for the score-only coefficient. Direct ODE integration converges to the former. The score ratio is approximately $200$, below the stated depth threshold $\kappa^*\approx665.67$, so that condition does not remove the example. This quantitative comparison uses the conventional VP score coefficient $|A_t|=1/2$. Independently of that choice, the score-zero point above proves that no scalar $A_t$ represents the full velocity as $A_ts_t$.
checks.repair:
Use the full probability-flow velocity in the local Taylor argument. For a general diffusion with drift $f_t$ and scalar diffusion coefficient $g_t$, set $v_t=f_t-g_t^2s_t/2$. Define $V_\perp=\mathbb E\|P^\perp v_t\|^2$ and $V_\parallel=\mathbb E\|P^\parallel v_t\|^2$. The stated directional Jacobian bounds, Taylor expansion and $(a+b)^2\le2(a^2+b^2)$ then give
$$\mathbb E\delta_\ell(t)^2\le2\bigl[\beta_\ell^2V_\perp+(1-\beta_\ell)^2V_\parallel\bigr]\Delta t^2+O(\Delta t^3).$$
This is a valid local replacement under the existing smoothness and remainder assumptions. If $V_\parallel>0$, the same algebraic comparison of block envelopes uses $V_\perp/V_\parallel$ in place of the score ratio $\kappa_t$. The original score-based criterion and cache-stride certificate must therefore be re-established using the full velocity and the temporal assumptions. A variance-exploding, drift-free process could support a score-only step, but changing to that process would also require changing the specified kernel and the rest of the theory. The local replacement does not by itself recover the paper's complete caching guarantee.

checks.explanation: Exactness of a fully recomputed denoiser does not constrain cancellations between its internal blocks. Caching one block while recomputing another can break those cancellations by an arbitrary amount, without changing any posterior calculation in Theorem 1.
checks.demonstration:
Use the theorem’s scalar prior \(X_0\sim\tfrac12N(-2,1)+\tfrac12N(2,1)\), with total variance five. At \(\bar\alpha_\tau=1/2\), let \(M_t(x)=\mathbb E[X_0\mid X_t=x]\) be the exact denoiser. In particular,

\[M_\tau(y)=y/\sqrt2+\tanh(\sqrt2\,y).\]

Factor the exact denoiser into two blocks

\[h_1(x,t)=M_t(x)+K r(t),\qquad h_2(h,t)=h-Kr(t),\]

where \(r\) is smooth with \(r(\tau)=1\) and \(r(0)=0\). Full recomputation always gives \(M_t(x)\), for every finite \(K\). Freeze the first block from \(\tau\) to the terminal step while recomputing the second. The output becomes \(M_\tau(X_\tau)+K\). Posterior-error orthogonality gives

\[\mathbb E[X_0-M_\tau(X_\tau)-K]^2=\operatorname{MMSE}_\tau+K^2.\]

The theorem’s frozen-estimate ceiling is \(\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_c=2.5\); choosing \(K=10\) makes the reused output’s MSE at least 100. The example tests what the posterior theorem alone controls, not the paper’s particular implemented blocks or cache schedule.
checks.repair:
Retain Theorem 1 as a frozen-estimator result and motivation. A block-reuse theorem needs an additional approximation and propagation bound. For example, at a common forward-distributed input, suppose the cached-versus-fresh intermediate feature has RMS error at most \(\delta\), and the remaining decoder is \(L\)-Lipschitz. Its output differs from the exact posterior mean by RMS at most \(L\delta\); Minkowski gives

\[\sqrt{\mathbb E\|X_0-\widehat X_0^{\mathrm{reuse}}\|^2}\le\sqrt{\operatorname{MMSE}_t}+L\delta.\]

Prove such a feature bound for the actual reuse interval and account separately for the approximate sampler’s changed input distribution and trajectory. The posterior theorem alone supplies none of those block or trajectory controls.
checks.scope: The finding is the unsupported transfer from a valid frozen posterior estimate to partially stale internal computation. The formal MMSE result, its explicit Gaussian qualifications and the empirical cache-quality observations are not refuted by this factorization.

checks.claim: Prop 2: for any strictly increasing link, minimising the pairwise logistic loss recovers the h_G ordering.
checks.explanation: The proof identifies the minimizer over shared item scores with independently optimized pairwise probabilities. A scalar score must use consistent differences across all pairs; fitting the correct decision boundary does not ensure that it can realize all pair probabilities.
checks.demonstration: Write \(\psi=\operatorname{logit}\circ\Lambda\). The asserted identity \(s_i-s_j=\psi(h_i-h_j)\) forces \(\psi(a+b)=\psi(a)+\psi(b)\) along every three-item chain, which a general increasing link does not satisfy. More strongly, the saved probit example reverses two items. Set \(\Lambda(x)=\Phi(6x)\) and \((h_C,h_E,h_A,h_B)=(0,0.25,0.5,0.55)\). Give weight one to pairs \(CE,CA,EB\), and initially zero to the other three pairs. This connected tree has the unique population optimum, after fixing \(s_C=0\), \[s_E=\psi(0.25),\qquad s_A=\psi(0.5),\qquad s_B=\psi(0.25)+\psi(0.30).\] Here \(s_A\approx6.606>s_B\approx5.926\), despite \(h_A<h_B\). The finite optimum and its positive-definite Hessian on the anchored score space imply continuity when sufficiently small positive weights are added to the other pairs. Thus the reversal persists with non-degenerate coverage. The saved all-positive control uses weight \(10^{-3}\) on those pairs and gives approximately \((0,2.641,6.418,5.938)\). Free item scores can represent the correct decision boundary, so assumption A2 is satisfied.
checks.repair: One sufficient repair is logistic realizability: assume \(\Lambda(x)=\sigma(ax)\) with \(a>0\), and include scores \(s_i=ah_i+b\) in the model class. Each cross-entropy term is then minimized at its true pair probability. Connected positive pair coverage identifies all score differences, and the resulting order is the latent order. A theorem for other links requires a separate order-consistency argument under the actual pair-sampling design.
checks.scope: The failure concerns arbitrary monotone links with nonuniform pair sampling. It does not contradict the realizable logistic case or the saved uniform complete-pair control.

Let \(g_\ell\) be the population gradient on dataset \(\ell\) at a common reference, and give each branch one equal-size step \(\eta\). Then
\[\theta_k=\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}-\eta\sum_\ell p_{k\ell}g_\ell,\qquad \sum_k\alpha_k\theta_k=\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}-\eta\sum_\ell(\alpha P)_\ell g_\ell.\]
With \(P=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0.7&0.3\\0.3&0.7\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) and \(\alpha=(0.8,0.2)\), the effective weights are \((0.62,0.38)\). They differ from \(\alpha\), and distinct gradients make the parameter updates differ. By contrast, \(\alpha=(0.5,0.5)\) satisfies \(\alpha P=\alpha\) for the same genuinely mixed branches. For a particular \(\alpha\), the data weights coincide when \(\alpha P=\alpha\); coincidence for every simplex weight requires \(P=I\). Linearly dependent gradients can also make parameter updates coincide despite different data weights. Retain Eq. (7), which already propagates the composed mixtures.

checks.claim: The transformed-teacher Gaussian gradient has the displayed Hermite decomposition and Eq.154 vanishes for the even teacher.
checks.explanation: The transformed teacher is even, so its odd Hermite coefficients vanish. Its zeroth coefficient generally does not vanish. Multiplying it by a derivative of a quadratic activation produces a nonzero vector contribution, which equations (150) and (154) omit. This concerns the displayed Euclidean gradient identities, rather than a counterexample to the final rates.
checks.demonstration:
Let \(X\) be standard Gaussian in a task subspace, let \(\theta,w\) be unit vectors there, and write \(U=\theta^\top X\), \(V=w^\top X\), \(c=\theta^\top w\). Gaussian integration by parts gives
\[\mathbb E[F(U)VX]=c\,\mathbb E[F(U)(U^2-1)]\theta+\mathbb E[F(U)]w.\]
Thus evenness of \(F\) does not remove the second term. In the normalized Hermite notation of equation (150), the missing zeroth-index contribution is \(\sqrt2\,\bar\alpha_0\tilde\beta_{\kappa,2}\tilde w_\kappa\), multiplied by the displayed mixture factor.

The nonzero mean is compatible with the paper's teacher and clipping assumptions. Take the normalized even degree-four teacher \(R(U)=\pi_\kappa\mathrm{He}_4(U)/\sqrt{24}\), whose first nonzero Hermite degree is four. Set \(\tau=(\log d)^4\) and \(Z=\operatorname{clip}(R/\tau;\pm1/\log d)\). This is an allowed temperature choice. Gaussian polynomial tails make the clipping correction smaller than \(\tau^{-2}\); since \(\mathbb E R=0\) and \(\mathbb E R^2=\pi_\kappa^2\), Taylor expansion on the bounded range of \(Z\) gives
\[\mathbb E[Ze^Z]=\frac{\pi_\kappa^2}{\tau^2}+o(\tau^{-2})>0\]
for sufficiently large \(d\). Write \(F(U)=Z(U)e^{Z(U)}\).

For equation (154), choose an off-target neuron with \(w\perp\theta\) in a common task subspace; the source does not require task subspaces to be mutually orthogonal. Take zero bias and the effective activation
\[a_k\sigma_k(v)=\pi_k\left[\tfrac12\mathrm{He}_2(v)+0.01\bigl(\mathrm{He}_0(v)+\mathrm{He}_1(v)+\mathrm{He}_3(v)+\mathrm{He}_4(v)\bigr)\right].\]
All five required activation coefficients are nonzero and bounded above and below by fixed positive multiples of \(\pi_k\). The additional sign conditions concern target-task neurons. Here \(U,V\) are independent, \(\mathbb E[UF(U)]=0\), and \(\mathbb E[V(a_k\sigma_k)'(V)]=\pi_k\). Consequently the left side of equation (154) is exactly \(\lambda_\kappa\pi_k\mathbb E[F(U)]w\neq0\), while its right side is zero because \(\bar\alpha_1=0\). A tangent projection could remove a radial contribution, but it does not establish the printed unprojected equality.
checks.repair: Include the zeroth coefficient and other surviving correlated terms in the unprojected gradient. Derive any tangent-projected cancellation explicitly, and reprove the off-target bounds and final rates using the corrected gradient.

Among 550 records, let the first be \(E_{11}\) and the rest zero. In a neighboring dataset replace the second zero by \(-E_{11}+E_{22}\). The summed first-step direction changes from \(E_{11}\) to \(E_{22}\). Its top singular subspace therefore has projector \(E_{11}\) in one dataset and \(E_{22}\) in the other. Releasing the bases yields an event of probability one versus zero, requiring \(\delta\geq1\) for every finite \(\varepsilon\). Even if the bases are hidden, a nondegenerate continuous noisy scalar R gives final updates supported on two different diagonal lines. The pinned public training path computes ordinary gradients before constructing its privacy engine, consistent with this missing boundary.

Freezing or post-processing those outputs then preserves that guarantee.
